config.title: Bike Theft in Berlin - FAQ
config.subtitle: How many bikes go each year, the hour and district that decide your risk, whether a cellar helps, what the losses are worth, and what to do the morning it is gone.

items.q: How many bikes are stolen in Berlin?
items.a: Berlin police recorded **22,341 bike thefts in 2025**. That is down from **26,758 in 2024** and **34,136 in 2016**, so the number has fallen by about a third in a decade. Germany as a whole recorded 214,264 cases in 2025, which means Berlin accounts for more than ten per cent of the national total while holding under five per cent of the population.

items.q: Which Berlin district has the most bike theft?
items.a: By rate per resident, **Mitte** is highest at **1,068 reported thefts per 100,000 residents in 2025**, with Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg just behind at 1,005. **Spandau and Marzahn-Hellersdorf are lowest, both at 227.** Living in the inner city means roughly four and a half times the exposure of living at the edge, for the same bike and the same lock. By raw count Mitte is also first, with 4,243 cases in 2025.

items.q: What time of day do bikes get stolen in Berlin?
items.a: The hour in a police report is the **start of the offence window**, which is when the owner last saw the bike, not when a thief turned up. Read as a parking clock across 16,153 reports in the twelve months to 31 August 2026, **31% of losses were locked up between 18:00 and 22:00**, 25% between 14:00 and 18:00, 16% in each of the two morning bands, and only 11% between 22:00 and 06:00. The after-work bike is the exposed one.

items.q: Is a bike safe in a Berlin cellar or bike room?
items.a: Safer, not safe. **5.1% of reported Berlin bike thefts came out of a cellar or a bike room** rather than off the street, and the share is very uneven: **2.6% in Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg but 11.4% in Spandau**, and 8.5% in both Reinickendorf and Marzahn-Hellersdorf. In districts built around large blocks with shared basement storage, lock the frame to something fixed once it is downstairs.

items.q: How long does a bike have to stand before it is stolen?
items.a: Not long. **32% of reported thefts happened inside an offence window of three hours or less, and 12% inside a single hour.** In Neukölln the three-hour share reaches 39%. This is the argument against keeping a good lock for the long stand and a thin cable for the errand: the errand is where a third of the losses happen.

items.q: What is a stolen Berlin bike usually worth?
items.a: The **median value declared to the police was €900** and the mean was **€1,299**. **46% of stolen bikes were declared at €1,000 or more,** and in Mitte that share is 51%. Household contents insurance is where this lands in Germany. Before you need it, check three things in your own policy: whether theft away from home is covered at all, what the compensation cap is, and whether there is a night-time clause.

items.q: What do I do if my bike is stolen in Berlin?
items.a: Report it online through the **Polizei Berlin Internetwache**, which does not require a trip to a station. You will need the **frame number**, the make, roughly what it was worth, and the window between when you last saw the bike and when you found it gone. Without a report there is no insurance claim and no way to match the bike to you if it surfaces. If a GPS tracker shows you where it is, call the police on 110 rather than going to get it.

items.q: Does getting a bike coded in Berlin help?
items.a: It helps at the return end more than the theft end. A coding puts an owner code on the frame, which makes the bike harder to sell on and lets the police give it back if it is recovered. The **ADFC** and the police run coding appointments in Berlin. Pair it with writing down the frame number, which is stamped on the frame under the bottom bracket, or with the free Fahrradpass app from the German police prevention service.

items.q: Is there secure bike parking at Berlin stations?
items.a: At a small number of stations, through the **Bike+Ride** programme of secured collective lock-ups and individual boxes. There is much less than the city needs: infraVelo estimates **42,000 additional spaces are required at public transport stations by 2030**. A bike parking garage with more than 1,100 spaces is under construction at **Schöneweide** and one is in planning at Mahlsdorf, but garages at **Ostkreuz, Haselhorst and Landsberger Allee** passed their feasibility studies and are not being pursued because funding for further planning is not secured.
